name: island-food-web
title: Trophic structure restores the species-area law
question:
Does replacing the random interaction matrix with a trophic food web
(producers -> primary -> secondary consumers, antisymmetric predator-prey
couplings) change whether the model reproduces the classic species-area
relationship of island biogeography?
hypothesis:
Antisymmetric predator-prey interactions stabilise coexistence (a predator's
gain is its prey's loss, so no single species runs away), so larger islands —
with more carrying capacity to support more trophic links — should sustain
MORE species. The food-web variant should therefore show a POSITIVE
richness-vs-area correlation (recovering the MacArthur-Wilson species-area law)
and support higher equilibrium richness than the random-competition archipelago
of Study 1 at matched parameters.
objective:
Run the `island_food_web` composite across a seed ensemble and measure
(a) the across-island correlation of equilibrium richness with log-area and
(b) mean equilibrium richness, comparing against a matched-parameter
`island_archipelago` (random matrix) run.
description:
Faithful port of experiments/island_food_web.py (generate_food_web +
generate_interaction_matrix_from_food_web). The ONLY change from Study 1 is
the interaction matrix; the islands, migration coupler, and dynamics are
identical. The contrast isolates interaction STRUCTURE as the cause of the
species-area law: random competition (Study 1) destroys it, trophic structure
(this study) restores it.

expected_behavior.name: food-web-recovers-species-area
expected_behavior.en:
With trophic interactions, equilibrium species richness INCREASES with
island area: the across-island richness-vs-log-area correlation is clearly
positive (measured ~ +0.50), recovering the classic species-area law.
expected_behavior.rationale:
Antisymmetric predator-prey couplings prevent competitive runaway, so the
extra carrying capacity of larger islands supports additional coexisting
species rather than just more individuals of a winner.

expected_behavior.name: trophic-coexistence-exceeds-random
expected_behavior.en:
The food-web variant sustains higher mean equilibrium richness than the
random-competition archipelago (Study 1) at matched parameters.
expected_behavior.rationale:
Predator-prey stabilisation vs competitive exclusion: the same islands,
migration, and capacities, differing only in interaction structure, should
hold more species under a food web.

behavior_tests.name: food-web-recovers-species-area
behavior_tests.description: Ensemble across-island corr(richness, log area) must exceed 0.2.

provenance.note:
Measured ~ +0.50 (8-island, 30-species, 6-seed ensemble, 150
generations). 0.2 is a conservative positive floor that still fails if
the species-area signal collapsed.

behavior_tests.name: trophic-coexistence-exceeds-random
behavior_tests.description:
Ensemble mean equilibrium richness of the food-web variant minus that of the
matched random-matrix archipelago must exceed 0.5 species.

provenance.note:
Measured gain ~ +1.8 species (food web ~3.8 vs random ~1.95, matched
params). The ordering — not an exact gap — is the falsifiable signature.

pipeline_gate.proceed_condition:
island-food-web is the investigation's capstone contrast; it depends on the
random-competition baseline established by island-archipelago.

canonical_runs.name: default
canonical_runs.label: Food-web archipelago vs random competition (8 islands, 30 species, 6 seeds)
